/resources/ai-data-readiness.title: Enterprise AI Data Readiness Checklist
/resources/ai-data-readiness.h1: Is your enterprise data ready for an AI use case?
/resources/ai-data-readiness.desc: Assess data readiness for enterprise AI across relevance, quality, access, traceability, freshness and ownership before selecting a platform or model.

sections.h: Is your enterprise data ready for an AI use case?
p: Data readiness is specific to the task. A dataset can support reporting yet be unsuitable for an AI assistant that serves a different audience or makes a different decision. Start with the intended workflow, then assess whether the available information can support it safely and reliably.

sections.h: 1. Define the task and the information it needs
p: List the questions the application should answer or actions it should support. Identify the records, documents and system context needed for each task. Include difficult and uncommon examples. This creates a basis for assessing coverage instead of treating the size of a data collection as proof of usefulness.

Review completeness, accuracy, duplicates and conflicting definitions. For documents, check ownership, versioning and whether obsolete material can be excluded. Define how current the information needs to be for the task and how updates or deletions reach the AI application. A retrieval system can return a well-written answer from an outdated source.

Confirm who may access the source and whether the intended AI processing is permitted under organizational policies and agreements. Preserve relevant user permissions when retrieving information. Consider sensitive fields, residency, retention and deletion requirements with the appropriate security, privacy and legal stakeholders.

Retain identifiers and metadata that connect an answer or derived record to its source. Where an assistant cites material, test whether the citation actually supports the answer. Define how users report incorrect information and which owner can correct the underlying source rather than only changing a prompt.

Name the people responsible for the source, pipeline, access rules and application. Agree monitoring for failed updates, quality regressions and permission changes. Begin with a representative sample and record gaps before deciding whether a broader data platform program is necessary. The output should be a task-specific readiness assessment and prioritized remediation plan, not a claim that all enterprise data is ready for every AI use.

/resources/enterprise-ai-evaluation.title: Enterprise AI Agent Evaluation Checklist
/resources/enterprise-ai-evaluation.h1: How to evaluate an enterprise AI agent before release
/resources/enterprise-ai-evaluation.desc: Plan enterprise AI agent evaluation across task success, data permissions, tool actions, human escalation, operating cost and production monitoring.

sections.h: How to evaluate an enterprise AI agent before release
p: An agent that completes a demonstration is not automatically ready for production. Evaluation should test the agreed task, the information it can access and the actions it can take. Use representative evidence and explicit acceptance criteria to make the release decision with business, engineering and risk owners.

Collect normal requests, ambiguous instructions, missing information and cases outside the intended scope. Include examples from the people who perform the work today. Separate development examples from release evaluation where practical, and document what constitutes correct completion or an appropriate refusal.

For generated answers, assess correctness and whether source material supports the claims. For actions, check inputs, authorization, record updates and side effects in a safe test environment. An accurate explanation does not prove that a transaction was completed correctly. Include partial failures, retries and duplicate-request handling.

Test attempts to access restricted information, follow instructions embedded in untrusted documents or invoke actions outside the approved scope. Enforce permission and transaction controls in the connected systems. Prompt instructions are one layer of the design, not a substitute for access control or approval rules.

Specify when the agent should ask for clarification, request approval or transfer the task. Confirm that a person receives enough context to continue safely. Define rollback or remediation for incorrect actions and establish who handles incidents. Test these paths rather than assuming that an escalation message is sufficient.

Assess response time, cost per completed task and behavior under expected load. After release, monitor failures, escalation patterns and user feedback alongside business outcomes. Re-evaluate when models, prompts, tools, knowledge or permissions change. The relevant tests differ for a CRM agent, a service workflow and a knowledge assistant; align the release criteria with the specific process.

/resources/forward-deployed-ai-vs-consul.h1: Forward deployed AI engineering, consulting or staff augmentation?
/resources/forward-deployed-ai-vs-consul.desc: Compare forward deployed AI engineering, consulting and staff augmentation by delivery responsibility, team structure and operational ownership.

sections.h: Forward deployed AI engineering, consulting or staff augmentation?
p: Choose an engagement model by the work you need completed and the responsibility you want the delivery partner to own. Strategy advice, additional engineering capacity and an embedded delivery pod solve different problems. An organization may use more than one model at different stages.

sections.h: Consulting: define the decision and direction
p: A consulting engagement can help assess readiness, prioritize use cases, compare architectures and create a roadmap. Its output may be a recommendation, operating model or implementation plan. Confirm whether hands-on implementation is included: the word consulting alone does not establish who will build or operate the solution.

sections.h: Staff augmentation: add capacity to your delivery team
p: Staff augmentation adds individual skills or capacity to a team that already owns the backlog, architecture and delivery process. It can fit a clearly defined engineering need where internal leaders can coordinate the work. Assess onboarding effort, supervision, access and continuity as well as the individual's skills.

sections.h: Forward deployed engineering: deliver alongside the business
p: An embedded engineering pod works close to process owners and technical teams to implement a scoped outcome. A useful pod combines the skills needed for the workflow, which may include data, AI, integration and evaluation. Define its backlog, acceptance criteria and responsibilities explicitly; the engagement label does not replace a delivery agreement.

sections.h: Questions to settle before selecting a model
p: Who owns the process and its success criteria? Are the data and environments accessible? Who approves design and release decisions? Who manages incidents and future model changes? If the team receiving the solution cannot operate it, include enablement and handover in the scope. Also agree whether ongoing support is included or separately commissioned.

sections.h: Evaluate proposals against the same milestones
p: Compare an assessment, a working demonstration, a production release and operational handover as separate deliverables. A demonstration may test feasibility without resolving permissions, scale or support. Ask each delivery partner to identify dependencies, excluded work, acceptance evidence and what happens when an assumption fails. Measure progress against accepted outcomes rather than activity alone.

faq: What makes data ready for AI?

AI-ready data is fit for a specific task: relevant, sufficiently accurate, accessible to authorized users and governed for the intended use. It also needs traceable sources and a plan for keeping it current. Readiness depends on the use case, not just where the data is stored.
Do we need a lakehouse before starting AI?

No single architecture is a prerequisite for every AI use case. An assessment should determine whether existing systems can provide the required data securely and reliably before recommending migration or a new platform.
How is this different from AI application development?

This practice builds and operates the data foundation. AI Services designs and evaluates the application or agent that uses it. A combined engagement is appropriate when both the data supply and the application need engineering.
Can we modernize incrementally?

Yes. A workload-based migration can move selected data products first, reconcile results against the existing system and expand after acceptance. Dependencies, cutover and rollback need to be planned for each stage.
How do we select a data platform?

Compare your workloads, integration requirements, security controls, team skills and total operating cost. Prolifics works with enterprise cloud and data platforms; platform choice should follow those requirements rather than precede them.

sections.h: FDE AI Engineering: frequently asked questions
faq: How does forward deployed AI engineering differ from consulting?

Consulting may focus on strategy and recommendations. A forward deployed engineering engagement includes hands-on implementation alongside your teams, with a defined backlog, acceptance criteria and operational responsibilities. Advisory work can be part of the engagement.
Is an FDE pod the same as staff augmentation?

Staff augmentation usually adds individual capacity to an existing team. An FDE pod is scoped around a delivery outcome and combines the skills needed to build, evaluate and operationalize it. Roles and accountability should be explicit in either model.
Do engineers have to work on site?

Working location and collaboration arrangements are agreed for the engagement. The essential requirement is close access to process owners, technical teams and approved environments, rather than a single mandatory location model.
Which engagement models are available?

Options include advisory, co-delivery, build-operate-transfer and managed services. Choose based on the capabilities you want to retain internally, the delivery scope and who will own ongoing operations.
How quickly can a pod start and deliver?

Timing depends on staffing, access, data readiness, integrations and approval requirements. Discovery establishes a realistic scope and sequence. A demonstration, production release and operational handover are separate milestones.
Who owns security and governance?

Responsibilities are agreed with your organization. The delivery design should cover least-privilege access, approved data use, evaluations, human approvals, incident handling and ownership after handover.

sections.h: Quality Engineering for Enterprise Applications & AI
p: Prolifics helps enterprises evaluate software quality across applications, integrations and AI-enabled workflows. Our quality engineering services combine test strategy, automation, functional and nonfunctional testing, and release evidence. We work with product, engineering and business teams to identify critical risks, define acceptance criteria and build repeatable checks into the delivery lifecycle.
Published by Prolifics · Updated 2 November 2026
For delivery leaders managing complex releases, platform changes or AI applications who need reliable test coverage, clear release evidence and a sustainable approach to quality.

sections.h: Evaluate the complete user and business journey

cards.d: Map critical workflows, select suitable automated checks and define test-data and environment needs. Maintain useful regression coverage as the application changes rather than maximizing test count alone.
Assess expected workload, response-time requirements and failure recovery. Use realistic load profiles and investigate system bottlenecks before setting a performance acceptance decision.
Combine automated checks with manual keyboard, screen-reader and interaction review for the agreed scope. Record reproducible issues and validate remediation with the relevant user journeys.

Evaluate task success, grounded answers, permissions, agent actions and human escalation. Include representative and difficult cases and define how evaluations will change with models, prompts and tools.

sections.h: Build evidence for a release decision

cards.d: Map important users, business transactions and failure consequences. Review the current defect history, delivery process and existing coverage with engineering and process owners.
Agree the scenarios, environments, data and responsibilities needed to evaluate those risks. Make release criteria explicit, including the handling of unresolved defects and known limitations.

Run functional, integration and nonfunctional checks at the appropriate stages. Report actionable failures with reproduction steps and supporting evidence, then retest fixes and affected regression paths.

Use escaped defects, test reliability and production feedback to revise coverage. Assign ownership for automation maintenance, test-data changes and evaluation updates rather than treating the suite as a one-time deliverable.

sections.h: Coverage depends on accessible environments and clear expectations
p: Bring representative workflows, requirements, known risks, application architecture and current release plans. Test environments need suitable data and authorized access to connected systems. Agree how sensitive information is handled and which dependencies may be simulated. Testing can provide evidence about defined risks and scenarios; the release decision still needs accountable business and technology owners.

sections.h: Example: a release spanning CRM and ERP
p: An illustrative regression plan could follow a customer order from Salesforce to SAP and its downstream reporting. Tests would check mapping, permissions, calculations and recovery from failed transactions. Performance and accessibility checks would address the relevant user-facing steps. This is an example of coverage design, not a claim about a specific client or a guaranteed reduction in defects.

sections.h: Agree the baseline before measuring the result
p: Select measures for the agreed scope and compare like-for-like work before and after release. Targets are set with your process owners; these measures are not promised customer results.
table: Whether critical journeys and failure paths have meaningful checks.

faq: How is quality engineering different from final-stage testing?

Quality engineering introduces risk analysis, testability and repeatable checks throughout delivery. Testing remains essential, but the approach also addresses environments, data, automation maintenance and feedback from production.
Should every test be automated?

No. Choose automation for repeatable checks where the value outweighs the maintenance cost. Exploratory testing, usability, accessibility interactions and changing requirements may need human judgment alongside automation.
Does an automated accessibility scan establish conformance?

No. Automated tools detect some issues, but a full assessment needs manual evaluation for the agreed accessibility standard and scope. Findings should include affected journeys and evidence of remediation.
What changes when testing AI applications?

In addition to conventional software testing, assess variability, answer support, model and tool behavior, permissions and unsafe actions. Evaluate against an agreed task set and review changes to models, prompts, tools and knowledge.
Can you support ongoing platform releases?

An ongoing testing scope can cover agreed applications and release cycles. Responsibilities for environment access, data, automation maintenance, defect triage and release approval are defined with the delivery teams.
